    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    What is the domain of h(x)=x+3h(x) = \sqrt{x + 3}h(x)=x+3​?

    Answer choices for question 3

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Solves x−3≥0x - 3 \ge 0x−3≥0, flipping the sign of the constant that sits inside the root.

    You chose B: Treats x+3x + 3x+3 as a denominator and throws out only the input that makes it zero, though a square root bars a whole side of the number line rather than a single value.

    You chose D: Requires the inside of the root to be at most zero, reversing the direction a real square root demands.

    A square root is a real number only when the quantity inside it is zero or positive, so the domain is every input satisfying that condition.

    x+3≥0  ⟹  x≥−3.x + 3 \ge 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x \ge -3.x+3≥0⟹x≥−3.

    Every input from −3-3−3 upward gives a real output, and every input below −3-3−3 gives none.

    Let f(x)=x+7f(x) = x + 7f(x)=x+7 and g(x)=x2−9g(x) = x^2 - 9g(x)=x2−9. Which inputs are excluded from the domain of fg\dfrac{f}{g}gf​?

    Answer choices for question 6

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Solves x2=9x^2 = 9x2=9 and keeps only the positive root, missing the negative input that also makes the denominator zero.

    You chose B: Throws out the input that makes the numerator zero; an output of 000 on top is a perfectly good value, and it is the denominator that may not vanish.

    You chose C: Assumes a quotient of two polynomial rules accepts every input, since neither rule has a denominator of its own.

    The quotient is undefined wherever the bottom function is zero, even where the top function is perfectly happy. So find every input with g(x)=0g(x) = 0g(x)=0.

    x2−9=0  ⟹  (x−3)(x+3)=0  ⟹  x=3  or  x=−3.x^2 - 9 = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; (x - 3)(x + 3) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x = 3 \ \text{ or } \ x = -3.x2−9=0⟹(x−3)(x+3)=0⟹x=3  or  x=−3.

    Advanced. This question goes beyond core Algebra I. It is not required by the course.

    A rule's graph is drawn below, crossed by one dashed vertical line and one dashed horizontal line. Taken together, what do the two line tests say about this graph?

    Answer choices for question 7

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Uses the horizontal line to decide whether the graph is a function at all; two horizontal crossings say the rule is not one-to-one, and it is the vertical line that answers the function question.

    You chose C: Reads the single vertical crossing as settling both questions, as if being a function also guaranteed that each output came from just one input.

    You chose D: Counts any meeting as a failure, though a vertical line meeting the graph exactly once is the vertical line test being passed.

    The two tests answer two different questions. The vertical line gathers every point sharing one input, and it meets this curve exactly once, so no input has two outputs and the graph is a function. The horizontal line gathers every point sharing one output, and it meets the curve twice, so two different inputs land on the same output.

    one vertical crossing⇒a function,two horizontal crossings⇒not one-to-one.\text{one vertical crossing} \Rightarrow \text{a function}, \qquad \text{two horizontal crossings} \Rightarrow \text{not one-to-one}.one vertical crossing⇒a function,two horizontal crossings⇒not one-to-one.

    A rule that is not one-to-one cannot be reversed, because the shared output would have to be sent back to two different inputs at once.

    A function fff has domain all numbers except 444, and its range is all numbers except 000. What are the domain and the range of f−1f^{-1}f−1?

    Answer choices for question 11

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Copies both sets straight across, though the inverse reverses every pair, so what was a set of inputs becomes a set of outputs.

    You chose C: Trades the domain correctly but then reads the range off the same set, taking both from the range of fff.

    You chose D: Negates the excluded value, as if reversing a function also reversed the sign of the numbers it bars.

    The inverse turns each pair (input, output) of fff into the pair (output, input). So the numbers that were outputs of fff are the inputs of f−1f^{-1}f−1, and the numbers that were inputs of fff are its outputs.

    domain of f−1=range of f,range of f−1=domain of f.\text{domain of } f^{-1} = \text{range of } f, \qquad \text{range of } f^{-1} = \text{domain of } f.domain of f−1=range of f,range of f−1=domain of f.

    The two sets trade places, so f−1f^{-1}f−1 has domain all numbers except 000 and range all numbers except 444.

    Solution

    a⋆e=a+e−6=a  ⟹  e=6,6⋆a=6+a−6=a.a \star e = a + e - 6 = a \;\Longrightarrow\; e = 6, \qquad 6 \star a = 6 + a - 6 = a.a⋆e=a+e−6=a⟹e=6,6⋆a=6+a−6=a.

    So 666 works from both sides. The other three fail: 3a+e=a3a + e = a3a+e=a forces e=−2ae = -2ae=−2a, which is not a fixed number; a△1=a+1≠aa \triangle 1 = a + 1 \neq aa△1=a+1=a; and a−e=aa - e = aa−e=a gives e=0e = 0e=0, yet 0−a=−a0 - a = -a0−a=−a, so subtraction has no identity on the left.

    10 pts

    A single rule, f(x)=2x2−5f(x) = 2x^2 - 5f(x)=2x2−5, is put to work below at two numbers and once at an expression.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Find f(4)f(4)f(4) and f(−4)f(-4)f(−4).

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 3 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Find f(t+1)f(t + 1)f(t+1), expanded and simplified.

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Compare the two outputs you computed in part A. Explain what that comparison does, or does not, show about whether fff is a function, and state what a rule would have to do to fail the definition.

      Carry your own answer forward Argue from the two outputs you computed in part A, whatever they came out to be.

      Explain why it works A sentence or two. Reasons, not steps. 3 points

    The answer

    Part A

    f(4)=27f(4) = 27f(4)=27 and f(−4)=27f(-4) = 27f(−4)=27.

    Part B

    f(t+1)=2t2+4t−3f(t + 1) = 2t^2 + 4t - 3f(t+1)=2t2+4t−3.

    Part C

    The two outputs match, and that shows nothing against fff: the definition restricts each input to one output and says nothing about outputs being shared. A rule fails only when a single input is assigned two different outputs.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Replace xxx by each input in turn, keeping the parentheses so the sign is squared along with the digit.

    f(4)=2(4)2−5=32−5=27,f(−4)=2(−4)2−5=32−5=27.f(4) = 2(4)^2 - 5 = 32 - 5 = 27, \qquad f(-4) = 2(-4)^2 - 5 = 32 - 5 = 27.f(4)=2(4)2−5=32−5=27,f(−4)=2(−4)2−5=32−5=27.

    Squaring removes the sign before the doubling and the subtraction happen, so the two inputs land on the same output.

    Part B

    The input is the whole expression t+1t + 1t+1, so all of it goes into the square.

    f(t+1)=2(t+1)2−5=2(t2+2t+1)−5=2t2+4t+2−5=2t2+4t−3.f(t + 1) = 2(t + 1)^2 - 5 = 2(t^2 + 2t + 1) - 5 = 2t^2 + 4t + 2 - 5 = 2t^2 + 4t - 3.f(t+1)=2(t+1)2−5=2(t2+2t+1)−5=2t2+4t+2−5=2t2+4t−3.

    The middle term 4t4t4t comes from squaring the whole input; squaring only the ttt would lose it.

    Part C

    A function assigns to each input exactly one output. Two different inputs arriving at the same output are two separate pairs, and each still has a single result.

    4↦27and−4↦274 \mapsto 27 \quad \text{and} \quad -4 \mapsto 274↦27and−4↦27

    Neither input is ambiguous, so the definition is satisfied. What the definition forbids is the reverse: one input with two outputs, as in the rule that sends 999 to both 333 and −3-3−3 because both square to 999. That is the only way to fail.

    In one line

    f(4)=27f(4) = 27f(4)=27 and f(−4)=27f(-4) = 27f(−4)=27, and f(t+1)=2t2+4t−3f(t + 1) = 2t^2 + 4t - 3f(t+1)=2t2+4t−3. The repeated output is harmless: a function may send two different inputs to one output, and it fails the definition only when one input is given two different outputs.

    Part A

    f−1(x)=4x+12f^{-1}(x) = 4x + 12f−1(x)=4x+12.

    Part B

    f−1(5)=32f^{-1}(5) = 32f−1(5)=32, and f(32)=8−3=5f(32) = 8 - 3 = 5f(32)=8−3=5, the number the inverse was handed.

    1f(5)=−47\dfrac{1}{f(5)} = -\dfrac{4}{7}f(5)1​=−74​. The inverse answers which input fff turns into 555; the reciprocal answers what one divided by the output at 555 comes to. The two questions are unrelated.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Write y=x4−3y = \dfrac{x}{4} - 3y=4x​−3, swap the two letters so the output becomes the input, and then solve for yyy.

    x=y4−3  ⟹  x+3=y4  ⟹  y=4(x+3)=4x+12.x = \frac{y}{4} - 3 \;\Longrightarrow\; x + 3 = \frac{y}{4} \;\Longrightarrow\; y = 4(x + 3) = 4x + 12.x=4y​−3⟹x+3=4y​⟹y=4(x+3)=4x+12.

    The rule divides by 444 and then subtracts 333; the undo adds 333 and then multiplies by 444, with the steps reversed and each one turned around.

    Part B

    Evaluate the inverse at 555.

    f−1(5)=4(5)+12=32.f^{-1}(5) = 4(5) + 12 = 32.f−1(5)=4(5)+12=32.

    A correct inverse must send 555 back to the input that fff turns into 555, so run fff forwards on the result.

    f(32)=324−3=8−3=5.f(32) = \frac{32}{4} - 3 = 8 - 3 = 5.f(32)=432​−3=8−3=5.

    The round trip closes, which is what confirms the value.

    Part C

    Evaluate fff at 555 first, then take the reciprocal of that output.

    f(5)=54−3=−74,1f(5)=−47.f(5) = \frac{5}{4} - 3 = -\frac{7}{4}, \qquad \frac{1}{f(5)} = -\frac{4}{7}.f(5)=45​−3=−47​,f(5)1​=−74​.

    Set that beside the value of f−1(5)f^{-1}(5)f−1(5) from part B. The two are nowhere near each other, and they are not supposed to be. The inverse runs the rule backwards and hands back the input that produced a given output. The reciprocal runs the rule forwards and then flips the output into a fraction. The raised −1-1−1 marks the inverse under composition, not a division.

      Part C.

      The input −13-\tfrac{1}{3}−31​ makes fff zero. Decide whether it belongs to the domain of fg\dfrac{f}{g}gf​, and justify your verdict by contrasting it with an input that makes ggg zero.

    The answer

    Part A

    (f+g)(x)=x2+3x−24(f + g)(x) = x^2 + 3x - 24(f+g)(x)=x2+3x−24 and (f−g)(x)=−x2+3x+26(f - g)(x) = -x^2 + 3x + 26(f−g)(x)=−x2+3x+26.

    Part B

    (fg)(x)=3x+1x2−25\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)(x) = \dfrac{3x + 1}{x^2 - 25}(gf​)(x)=x2−253x+1​, and it excludes x=5x = 5x=5 and x=−5x = -5x=−5.

    Part C

    It does belong: it makes only the top zero, so the quotient has the value 000 there. An input that makes ggg zero, such as 555, is excluded instead, because a division by zero has no value at all.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Evaluate both rules at the same input and combine the outputs.

    (f+g)(x)=(3x+1)+(x2−25)=x2+3x−24.(f + g)(x) = (3x + 1) + (x^2 - 25) = x^2 + 3x - 24.(f+g)(x)=(3x+1)+(x2−25)=x2+3x−24.

    (f−g)(x)=(3x+1)−(x2−25)=3x+1−x2+25=−x2+3x+26.(f - g)(x) = (3x + 1) - (x^2 - 25) = 3x + 1 - x^2 + 25 = -x^2 + 3x + 26.(f−g)(x)=(3x+1)−(x2−25)=3x+1−x2+25=−x2+3x+26.

    The subtraction reaches every term of ggg, which is why the −25-25−25 arrives as +25+25+25.

    Part B

    The quotient puts fff's output over ggg's output.

    (fg)(x)=3x+1x2−25.\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)(x) = \frac{3x + 1}{x^2 - 25}.(gf​)(x)=x2−253x+1​.

    It has no value at any input where the bottom rule is zero, so solve that.

    x2−25=0  ⟹  (x−5)(x+5)=0  ⟹  x=5  or  x=−5.x^2 - 25 = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; (x - 5)(x + 5) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x = 5 \ \text{ or } \ x = -5.x2−25=0⟹(x−5)(x+5)=0⟹x=5  or  x=−5.

    Both inputs are thrown out, even though fff is perfectly happy at each of them.

    Part C

    A fraction is undefined only when its denominator is zero; a zero numerator is an ordinary value. At x=−13x = -\tfrac{1}{3}x=−31​ the denominator is 19−25\tfrac{1}{9} - 2591​−25, which is not zero.

    (fg)(−13)=019−25=0.\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)\left(-\tfrac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{0}{\tfrac{1}{9} - 25} = 0.(gf​)(−31​)=91​−250​=0.

    So that input is admitted, and its output happens to be 000. At x=5x = 5x=5 the denominator is 000, and no such division has a value, so that input is thrown out. A zero on top produces an output; a zero underneath produces none.

    In one line

    (f+g)(x)=x2+3x−24(f + g)(x) = x^2 + 3x - 24(f+g)(x)=x2+3x−24, (f−g)(x)=−x2+3x+26(f - g)(x) = -x^2 + 3x + 26(f−g)(x)=−x2+3x+26, and (fg)(x)=3x+1x2−25\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)(x) = \dfrac{3x + 1}{x^2 - 25}(gf​)(x)=x2−253x+1​ excluding x=5x = 5x=5 and x=−5x = -5x=−5. The input −13-\tfrac{1}{3}−31​ stays in the domain, with output 000, because only a zero denominator, never a zero numerator, destroys a quotient.

    7. Two orders, then a hunt for an identity . 11 points. This question goes beyond core Algebra I. It is not required by the course. Question 7 of 10.

    11 pts Advanced. This question goes beyond core Algebra I. It is not required by the course.

    An operation is defined by a⋆b=a+2b−aba \star b = a + 2b - aba⋆b=a+2b−ab. Its two slots are treated differently, so how it behaves in each slot is worth checking.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Compute 3⋆53 \star 53⋆5 and 5⋆35 \star 35⋆3, and say what the two results settle.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 3 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Find the only number eee for which a⋆e=aa \star e = aa⋆e=a holds for every aaa.

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Test that candidate on the other side, and state whether ⋆\star⋆ has an identity element.

      Carry your own answer forward Take the candidate you found in part B and place it in the FIRST slot instead.

      Construct a counterexample Give one specific case, and show it breaks the claim. 4 points

    The answer

    Part A

    3⋆5=−23 \star 5 = -23⋆5=−2 and 5⋆3=−45 \star 3 = -45⋆3=−4. The two orders disagree, so ⋆\star⋆ is not commutative.

    Part B

    e=0e = 0e=0.

    Part C

    0⋆5=100 \star 5 = 100⋆5=10, not 555, so the candidate fails from the left. In general 0⋆a=2a0 \star a = 2a0⋆a=2a, which returns the input only at a=0a = 0a=0, so ⋆\star⋆ has no identity element.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Put each pair into its slots in the order written, doing the multiplications before the additions.

    3⋆5=3+2(5)−(3)(5)=3+10−15=−2,3 \star 5 = 3 + 2(5) - (3)(5) = 3 + 10 - 15 = -2,3⋆5=3+2(5)−(3)(5)=3+10−15=−2,

    5⋆3=5+2(3)−(5)(3)=5+6−15=−4.5 \star 3 = 5 + 2(3) - (5)(3) = 5 + 6 - 15 = -4.5⋆3=5+2(3)−(5)(3)=5+6−15=−4.

    One disagreeing pair is enough: swapping the inputs can change the answer, so the operation is not commutative.

    Part B

    Substitute eee into the second slot and gather the terms that contain it.

    a⋆e=a+2e−ae=a  ⟹  2e−ae=0  ⟹  e(2−a)=0.a \star e = a + 2e - ae = a \;\Longrightarrow\; 2e - ae = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; e(2 - a) = 0.a⋆e=a+2e−ae=a⟹2e−ae=0⟹e(2−a)=0.

    A product is zero when one of its factors is. The factor 2−a2 - a2−a vanishes only at the single value a=2a = 2a=2, so it cannot deliver the condition for every aaa; the other factor must be the one that vanishes, forcing e=0e = 0e=0. Checking on that side: a⋆0=a+0−0=aa \star 0 = a + 0 - 0 = aa⋆0=a+0−0=a.

    Part C

    An identity has to leave every input unchanged from both sides. Put the candidate in the first slot.

    0⋆a=0+2a−(0)(a)=2a.0 \star a = 0 + 2a - (0)(a) = 2a.0⋆a=0+2a−(0)(a)=2a.

    That returns aaa only when a=0a = 0a=0, and one counterexample finishes it.

    0⋆5=10≠5.0 \star 5 = 10 \neq 5.0⋆5=10=5.

    The candidate survives one side and fails the other, which is exactly the risk part A flagged: because the operation is not commutative, passing on the right says nothing about the left. Part B showed 000 was the only candidate even on the right, so no number works on both sides and ⋆\star⋆ has no identity element.

    In one line

    3⋆5=−23 \star 5 = -23⋆5=−2 while 5⋆3=−45 \star 3 = -45⋆3=−4, so ⋆\star⋆ is not commutative. The condition a⋆e=aa \star e = aa⋆e=a forces e=0e = 0e=0, but 0⋆a=2a0 \star a = 2a0⋆a=2a, which already fails at a=5a = 5a=5. So ⋆\star⋆ has no identity element, and because the operation is not commutative, passing on one side could never have settled the other.

    P(r(m))=8m+204−1=2m+4P(r(m)) = \dfrac{8m + 20}{4} - 1 = 2m + 4P(r(m))=48m+20​−1=2m+4.

    131313 kilograms.

    The inverse is x−42\dfrac{x - 4}{2}2x−4​. Its input is a display reading and its output is the mass in kilograms that produced it. The composite took masses in and gave readings out, so reversing it swaps those roles.

    Part A

    The scale runs first, so its whole rule drops into the display's input slot.

    P(r(m))=8m+204−1=(2m+5)−1=2m+4.P(r(m)) = \frac{8m + 20}{4} - 1 = (2m + 5) - 1 = 2m + 4.P(r(m))=48m+20​−1=(2m+5)−1=2m+4.

    Its input is a percentage shown on the display, and its output is the mass in kilograms behind that reading. Those roles are forced rather than chosen: the composite's inputs were masses and its outputs were readings, and an inverse turns each pair (mass, reading) into the pair (reading, mass). So the inverse's domain is the set of readings and its range is the set of masses, exactly the trade the swap performs. Part B was this inverse used once, taking the reading 303030 and returning the mass 131313.

    3. C
      Part C.

      Taken on its own, the simplified rule from part B is defined at every real number. Explain why it is still not the same function as fff, and name the single input-output pair that one of the two owns and the other does not.

      Carry your own answer forward Use the excluded input and the unreachable output you identified in part B.

      Explain why it works A sentence or two. Reasons, not steps. 3 points

    The answer

    Part A

    f(3)=−2f(3) = -2f(3)=−2 and f(−1)=−6f(-1) = -6f(−1)=−6.

    Part B

    f(x)=x−5f(x) = x - 5f(x)=x−5 at every input except x=−5x = -5x=−5, and the output −10-10−10 is never produced.

    Part C

    They agree everywhere fff is defined, but the simplified rule accepts one input more. It owns the pair (−5,−10)(-5, -10)(−5,−10), which fff does not, and a function is the pairing of inputs with outputs it carries, so the two are different functions however alike the formulas look.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Substitute each input into the top and the bottom, then divide.

    f(3)=32−253+5=−168=−2,f(−1)=(−1)2−25−1+5=−244=−6.f(3) = \frac{3^2 - 25}{3 + 5} = \frac{-16}{8} = -2, \qquad f(-1) = \frac{(-1)^2 - 25}{-1 + 5} = \frac{-24}{4} = -6.f(3)=3+532−25​=8−16​=−2,f(−1)=−1+5(−1)2−25​=4−24​=−6.

    Part B

    Factor the top and divide out the common factor, remembering that the division was only ever available where the bottom is not zero.

    x2−25x+5=(x−5)(x+5)x+5=x−5,x≠−5.\frac{x^2 - 25}{x + 5} = \frac{(x - 5)(x + 5)}{x + 5} = x - 5, \qquad x \neq -5.x+5x2−25​=x+5(x−5)(x+5)​=x−5,x=−5.

    The refused input is −5-5−5, where the original denominator vanishes. For the outputs: at every input it does accept, fff behaves exactly like x−5x - 5x−5, and x−5x - 5x−5 reaches −10-10−10 only at x=−5x = -5x=−5. That input is unavailable, so −10-10−10 is the one number fff never returns.

    Part C

    A function is settled by which inputs it accepts and what it returns for each, not by how its formula is written. Compare the two at the one input where they can differ.

    the simplified rule sends −5↦−10,f gives −5 no output at all.\text{the simplified rule sends } -5 \mapsto -10, \qquad f \text{ gives } -5 \text{ no output at all.}the simplified rule sends −5↦−10,f gives −5 no output at all.

    Everywhere else the two agree exactly. But the simplified rule owns the pair (−5,−10)(-5, -10)(−5,−10), which fff does not, so the two collections of pairs are different and the rules are different functions. That single missing pair is also why −10-10−10 never appears among fff's outputs. Cancelling a common factor rewrites how a rule looks; it cannot hand back an input the original rule never accepted.

    In one line

    f(3)=−2f(3) = -2f(3)=−2 and f(−1)=−6f(-1) = -6f(−1)=−6. The rule simplifies to x−5x - 5x−5 at every input except −5-5−5, and the single output it never produces is −10-10−10. It is not the same function as x−5x - 5x−5 taken on its own, which owns the pair (−5,−10)(-5, -10)(−5,−10), because a function is decided by the pairs it holds rather than by the appearance of its formula.

    Mark your own paper against this. Give yourself the points for each element you actually wrote down, not the ones you meant to.

    2

    Part C 3 points
